h: Aufbau dieser Hilfe Hilfe in TraceDraw Wo Sie anfangen
x: Willkommen in der TraceDraw-Hilfe TraceDraw ist ein freies, quelloffenes Vektorzeichenprogramm. Damit zeichnen Sie Illustrationen, Logos, Diagramme, Layouts und Druckarbeiten aus Formen, Linien und Text, die in jeder Größe scharf bleiben, und kombinieren sie mit Bitmaps. Dasselbe Programm läuft unter Windows, macOS und Linux und im Webbrowser. Diese Hilfe erklärt Schritt für Schritt, wie Sie in TraceDraw arbeiten, und was jedes Dialogfeld, jedes Andockfenster und jedes Werkzeug tut. Aufbau dieser Hilfe Das Inhaltsverzeichnis links folgt Ihrer Arbeitsweise: Erste Schritte stellt den Arbeitsbereich, neue Zeichnungen, Öffnen und Speichern vor. Linien, Formen und Umrisse, Objekte, Symbole und Ebenen und Farben, Füllungen und Transparenzen behandeln das Zeichnen und Anordnen von Objekten. Spezialeffekte, Text, Vorlagen und Stile, Seiten und Layout und Bitmaps decken die übrige Zeichenarbeit ab. Drucken, Webgrafiken und Dateiformate erklären, wie Ihre Arbeit aus TraceDraw herauskommt. Anpassen und automatisieren behandelt die Optionen, Arbeitsbereiche, Skripte und KI-Funktionen, und Referenz listet jeden Menübefehl, jedes Werkzeug, jedes Andockfenster und jedes Tastenkürzel auf. Mit der Registerkarte Suchen finden Sie eine Seite über jedes Wort, das sie enthält, und mit der Sprachliste oben lesen Sie dieselbe Seite in einer anderen Sprache. Hilfe in TraceDraw Drücken Sie F1, um die Seite zu dem zu öffnen, was gerade vor Ihnen liegt: das geöffnete Dialogfeld, sonst das angezeigte Andockfenster, sonst das aktive Werkzeug. Klicken Sie auf die Schaltfläche ? unten in einem Dialogfeld oder einer Optionsseite, um deren Seite zu öffnen. Wählen Sie Hilfe > Hilfethemen, um diese Seite zu öffnen. Das Andockfenster Hinweise beschreibt beim Arbeiten das aktive Werkzeug; sein Link Mehr erfahren öffnet hier die Seite des Werkzeugs. Siehe Hinweise. Die Seiten öffnen sich in Ihrem Webbrowser, in der Sprache, auf die TraceDraw eingestellt ist. Wo Sie anfangen Wenn TraceDraw neu für Sie ist, lesen Sie Der Arbeitsbereich, dann Eine Zeichnung anlegen und Linien und Kurven zeichnen.

h: Neues im Programm sehen Highlights der letzten Versionen
x: Neuigkeiten Jede Version von TraceDraw bringt Funktionen und Korrekturen. Diese Seite erklärt, wie Sie herausfinden, was sich geändert hat, und nennt die Highlights der letzten Versionen. Neues im Programm sehen Wählen Sie Hilfe > Neue Funktionen, um die Seite mit den Neuigkeiten des Begrüßungsbildschirms für diese Version zu öffnen. Schalten Sie Hilfe > Neue Funktionen hervorheben ein, um in den Menüs zu markieren, was in dieser Version neu ist: Ein kleiner Punkt erscheint am Ende jedes neuen Befehls, neben dem Pfeil eines Untermenüs, das zu einem führt, und über dem Titel eines Menüs, das einen enthält. Die Markierungen verschwinden, wenn Sie den Befehl ausschalten, und beim nächsten Start von TraceDraw ist der Befehl wieder aus. Die vollständige Liste der Änderungen jeder Version steht im Änderungsprotokoll des Projekts. Highlights der letzten Versionen Objektminiaturen. Das Andockfenster Objekte zeigt jedes Objekt verkleinert neben seinem Namen; Strg+Mausrad über der Liste oder der Schieberegler unten stellt die Größe ein. Siehe Objekte und Ebenen ordnen. Hilfe in Ihrer Sprache. Jede Schaltfläche ? und F1 öffnen die Seite dieser Hilfe zu dem Dialogfeld, Andockfenster oder Werkzeug vor Ihnen, in der Sprache, auf die TraceDraw eingestellt ist. Dokumenteigenschaften. Datei > Dokumenteigenschaften speichert Sprache, Titel, Betreff, Autor, Copyright, Stichwörter, Notizen und Bewertung einer Zeichnung, über einem vollständigen Bericht über ihren Inhalt. Siehe Dokumenteigenschaften. Farbmanagement. Extras > Farbverwaltung legt die Profile der Zeichnung und die Vorgaben für neue fest, mit Regeln für Dateien, die geöffnet oder importiert werden. Siehe Farbmanagement. Strichcodes und QR-Codes. Ein Assistent in drei Schritten platziert Strichcodes, und QR-Codes sind dynamische Objekte, die Sie im Andockfenster Eigenschaften bearbeiten. Siehe Strichcodes und QR-Codes. Effekte. Das Menü Effekte fasst die Effekt-Andockfenster zusammen; Überblendungen können einem Pfad mit festem Abstand folgen und ihre Farben im oder gegen den Uhrzeigersinn drehen. Siehe Überblendungen. Text auf Pfad hat eigene Einstellungen für Ausrichtung, Platzierung, Abstand und Versatz. Siehe Text hinzufügen und bearbeiten. Der Schriftmanager ordnet installierte Schriften, Ordner, Favoriten und Sammlungen. Siehe Schriften und Glyphen.

h: Das Fenster Info Nach Updates suchen Automatisch prüfen Der Begrüßungsbildschirm Community und Support
x: Über TraceDraw und Updates TraceDraw ist frei und quelloffen. Diese Seite erklärt, wie Sie sehen, welche Version Sie haben, wie Sie eine neuere bekommen und wo Sie Hilfe finden. Das Fenster Info Wählen Sie Hilfe > Info über TraceDraw, um die laufende Version, den Autor, die Lizenz, einen Link zum Quellcode und die Grundlagen des Programms zu sehen. Drücken Sie Schließen, Eingabe oder Esc, um es zu schließen.  Nach Updates suchen Auf dem Desktop kann TraceDraw Ihnen sagen, wenn eine neuere Version erschienen ist. So prüfen Sie jetzt: Wählen Sie Hilfe > Updates. TraceDraw fragt die Release-Seite des Projekts nach der neuesten Version und sagt, ob sie neuer ist als Ihre. Testversionen und nächtliche Builds werden nie angeboten. Wenn es eine neuere Version gibt, wählen Sie, was geschehen soll: Herunterladen öffnet den Download der Datei für Ihr System (das Installationsprogramm oder das portable Archiv unter Windows, das Disk-Image für den Prozessor Ihres Mac, das AppImage oder das Archiv unter Linux). Das Installationsprogramm Ihres Systems übernimmt dann die Installation. Versionshinweise öffnet die Liste der Änderungen dieser Version. Diese Version überspringen bietet diese Version nicht mehr an. Schließen schließt das Fenster. Wenn TraceDraw als Linux-AppImage läuft, kann das Fenster auch Installieren anbieten: Es lädt das neue AppImage neben das laufende herunter, prüft, dass der Download vollständig und echt ist, und setzt es an die Stelle der alten Datei. Die neue Version startet beim nächsten Öffnen von TraceDraw. Wenn etwas nicht stimmt, bleibt die alte Datei unverändert und das Fenster sagt Ihnen, warum. Wenn die Prüfung fehlschlägt (zum Beispiel ohne Internetverbindung), sagt das Fenster das und bietet die Release-Seite an.  Automatisch prüfen Extras > Optionen > Global, Seite Allgemein, hat eine Einstellung, um beim Start nach Updates zu suchen. Sie ist anfangs eingeschaltet: Einmal am Tag prüft TraceDraw beim Start im Stillen und meldet sich nur, wenn eine neuere Version vorliegt, die Sie nicht übersprungen haben. Beim ersten Start fragt TraceDraw, ob es nach Updates suchen soll: Immer prüfen oder Nie prüfen. Bis Sie antworten, baut TraceDraw von sich aus keine Verbindung auf. Die Antwort setzt diese Einstellung, die Sie hier jederzeit ändern können. Hinweis: Die Browserversion ist immer die neueste. Dort öffnet Hilfe > Updates die Release-Seite. Der Begrüßungsbildschirm Der Begrüßungsbildschirm ist die erste Registerkarte, wenn TraceDraw startet. Von dort legen Sie eine Zeichnung an, öffnen eine der zuletzt verwendeten Zeichnungen (jede mit einer Miniatur; Liste löschen vergisst sie), beginnen mit einer Vorlage, lesen die Neuigkeiten und finden Lernmaterial. Ist eine Seite höher als das Fenster (eine lange Liste zuletzt verwendeter Zeichnungen), rollt sie mit dem Mausrad oder ihrer Bildlaufleiste; die Reihe der Registerkarten oben bleibt stehen. Wählen Sie Hilfe > Willkommensbildschirm, um ihn zurückzuholen. Hilfe > Video-Lernprogramme, Schnellstartanleitung und Benutzerhandbuch öffnen seine Lernseite, Neue Funktionen seine Neuigkeiten. Community und Support Hilfe > Community öffnet das Diskussionsforum des Projekts, wo Sie Fragen stellen und Ideen teilen können. Hilfe > Support öffnet den Issue-Tracker, wo Sie ein Problem melden können. Hilfe > Nachrichteneinstellungen öffnet die Optionen, in denen die Meldungen von TraceDraw eingestellt werden.

Erste Schritte Diese Seiten stellen TraceDraw vor: die Teile des Fensters, wie Sie Zeichnungen anlegen, öffnen und speichern, wie Sie sich in einer Zeichnung bewegen und Arbeitsschritte rückgängig machen, und wo Sie beim Zeichnen Hilfe finden. TraceDraw läuft unter Windows, macOS und Linux sowie im Webbrowser, ohne dass etwas installiert werden muss. Beides ist dasselbe Programm; die wenigen Unterschiede der Browserversion erklärt Die Browserversion.

h: The parts of the window The standard toolbar The property bar The toolbox and flyouts Panels The drawing window The color palette The status bar Arranging the bars Working with several drawings The interface size
x: The workspace The TraceDraw window holds your drawings and everything you need to work on them. This page names its parts, so the other pages of this Help make sense. The parts of the window From top to bottom and from left to right: The menu bar holds every command, in the menus File, Edit, View, Layout, Object, Effects, Bitmaps, Text, Table, Tools, Window and Help. Each command shows its shortcut beside it. With no drawing open, only File, Tools, Window and Help are shown. The Menu commands page lists every command. The standard toolbar holds the common commands (see below). The property bar shows the settings of what you are doing now. The document tabs show one tab per open drawing. The toolbox, on the left, holds the tools. The rulers run along the top and the left of the drawing window. The drawing window shows the page on the desktop around it. The panels sit on the right. The color palette runs along the bottom. The status bar, at the very bottom, describes the active tool and the selection. The standard toolbar The standard toolbar holds, in groups: New, Open (its arrow lists the drawings you used last), Save and Print. Cut, Copy and Paste. Undo and Redo. Their arrows list the steps, so you can undo or redo several at once by choosing a step. Import, Export and Publish to PDF. The zoom box: type a zoom level and press Enter, or open its list for zoom to selected, to all objects, to the page, to the page width or height, and levels from 10% to 1600%. Then full-screen preview. Show rulers, show grid and show guidelines, drawn pressed while on. Snap off (Alt+Q) and the list of what to snap to. Options, which opens the list of option pages. Launch: Font Manager, Welcome Screen and Color Management. Hover a button to see its name, its shortcut and what it does. The property bar The property bar changes with what you do. With nothing selected and the Pick tool active, it shows the page size and orientation, the drawing units and the nudge distance. With objects selected, it shows their position, size, scale, rotation and mirror buttons, then the settings of that kind of object. Each tool adds its own settings, explained on the page of the tool. In number fields you can type a sum such as 10+5, or a value in another unit such as 1 in, which is converted to the drawing units. The toolbox and flyouts The toolbox has one button per group of tools. A button with a small arrow at its corner holds a flyout, a list of related tools. To open a flyout, click the arrow, right-click the button, or press and hold it. The button then shows the tool you used last from that group. Hover a tool to see its name, its shortcut and what it does. Double-clicking some buttons has a shortcut action: Pick selects all objects, Zoom zooms to fit all objects and Rectangle adds a rectangle the size of the page. The + button at the end of the toolbox lists the groups with a check box to show or hide each one, and resets the toolbox. The Toolbox page lists every tool. Panels Panels hold settings you keep open while you work, such as Properties, Objects and Hints, which are open at first. Open panels are tabs down the right side; click a tab to bring its panel to the front, or click the tab in front to fold the panels away. Open other panels from Window > Panels or with their shortcuts; the button with three dots under the tabs lists every panel, each with its picture, to show or hide it. When more panels are open than the column of tabs has room for, the column slides: use the arrows at its top and foot or the mouse wheel over it. Each panel has collapse and close buttons in its title bar. The Panels page lists every panel. The drawing window The page sits on the desktop, the area around it, where you can also keep objects. Below the drawing are: the page navigator: insert a page before, first page, previous page, the page number, next page, last page and insert a page after; one tab per page (click to go to a page, double-click to rename it); the horizontal scroll bar. Drag the dotted splitter between the page tabs and the scroll bar to share the space between them. The Navigator button in the corner between the scroll bars shows a thumbnail of the page while you hold it; move the pointer over the thumbnail to move the view. Double-clicking the page border with the Pick tool opens the page size options. The color palette Click a color of the palette to fill the selected objects; right-click it to color their outline. The document palette under the drawing window collects the colors your drawing uses. See Color palettes. The status bar The status bar shows a hint for the active tool, what is selected and on which layer, and the fill and outline of the selection. Double-click the fill or outline part to change them. The Status bar page explains each part. Arranging the bars You can move the toolbox, the color palette, the standard toolbar, the property bar and the status bar: drag a bar by its dotted grip to another edge of the window, or away from the edges to make it float. Right-click a grip to lock the bars or reset their positions. To show or hide a bar, use Window > Toolbars. You can also save the whole arrangement as a workspace; see Workspaces. The standard toolbar, the property bar, the Text, Zoom and Transform toolbars and the time tracker can share a row when docked at the top or the bottom: drag a toolbar's grip onto another toolbar's row to put it beside that one, or onto the line between two rows to give it a row of its own. The rows are kept with your preferences. A right click on any part of a docked bar opens its menu. Menus taller than the window scroll with the mouse wheel. Every slider in the bars, panels and dialog boxes works the same way: its label above it, a groove with tick marks, and the value in a box at the right that you can type into or step with its arrows. h: To create a drawing General Dimensions Color settings Skipping the dialog box Other ways to start
x: Creating a drawing Every drawing starts with a page size, a number of pages, a color mode and a resolution. You choose them in the Create a New Document dialog box. To create a drawing Choose File > New (Ctrl+N), click New on the standard toolbar, click the + after the last document tab, or click New Document on the Welcome Screen. In the Create a New Document dialog box, set the values described below. Click OK or press Enter. The drawing opens in its own tab. The dialog box remembers your values for the next drawing.  General Name names the drawing. It starts as the next Untitled-N. Preset sets the color mode, page size, units and resolution at once. The presets are TraceDraw default and Default CMYK (CMYK, A4, millimeters, 300 dpi), Default RGB (RGB, A4, millimeters, 300 dpi) and Web (RGB, 1920 x 1080 pixels, 72 dpi). When you change one of those values, the preset shows Custom unless the values match a preset again. The button beside the preset holds Save Preset, which asks for a Preset name and adds the current values to the list, and Delete Preset, which removes a preset you saved. The built-in presets cannot be deleted. Number of pages sets how many pages the drawing has, from 1 to 999. Each page is named "Page N" and has one layer. Primary color mode is CMYK, for print, or RGB, for screens. Dimensions Page size lists the paper sizes, or Custom. Choosing a size keeps the current orientation. A width and height you type that match a paper size, in either orientation, select its name. Width and Height set the page size, in the units you choose in the list beside the width. Those units become the drawing units of the property bar. Orientation: Portrait or Landscape. Resolution in dpi (300 at first). It is used for the effects that are turned into pixels, and to measure sizes in pixels: 1920 pixels are 162.56 mm at 300 dpi and 677.33 mm at 72 dpi. When the units are pixels, changing the resolution keeps the page's size in pixels. Color settings Open Color settings to choose the RGB profile, CMYK profile and Grayscale profile of the drawing and the Rendering intent. They start at sRGB, the built-in CMYK profile, a 20% dot gain grayscale and relative colorimetric. See Color management. Skipping the dialog box Tick Do not show this dialog again to create new drawings at once, with the values you used last. To see the dialog box again, turn on the matching setting on the General page of Tools > Options > TraceDraw. See TraceDraw options. Other ways to start File > New from Template starts from a template. See Templates. File > Open opens an existing drawing. See Opening and saving drawings.

h: Opening a drawing Notes after opening Saving a drawing Save As Closing drawings Auto-backup and recovery
x: Opening and saving drawings TraceDraw saves drawings in its own format, .tdraw, which keeps everything, and can also save .cdr files. It opens many other formats; see Supported file formats. Opening a drawing Choose File > Open (Ctrl+O), or click Open on the standard toolbar. Choose the file and confirm. The drawing opens in a new tab. To open a drawing you used recently, use File > Open Recent, the arrow of the Open button, or the list on the Welcome Screen; Clear list empties the list. To take one drawing off the Welcome Screen list, point at it and click the x at its right, or right-click it and choose Remove from list; the file itself stays where it is. File > Import (Ctrl+I) instead adds the content of a file to the drawing that is open; see Importing files. You can also drag files from your file manager onto TraceDraw. A drawing (such as a .tdraw or .cdr file) let go over the title bar, the menus, the toolbars or the document tabs opens in a tab of its own; let go over the drawing window, it is imported into the open drawing. The frame and the label shown while you drag say which will happen. Where the system does not say where the pointer is (Linux, macOS), drawings open in a tab and pictures are imported. How a drawing is first shown (the whole page, its objects, the page's width, real size, or the page, place and zoom it had when it was saved) is set by View when a drawing opens on the Display page of Tools > Options > TraceDraw. Notes after opening When some objects of an opened file could not be read, or the drawing uses fonts that are not installed on your computer, a message says so after the file opens: For objects that could not be read, it gives their number. A Report button opens a new issue for the file on the project's issue tracker, so the problem can be fixed. For missing fonts, the Missing Fonts dialog box lists them, each with the installed font that draws it, and lets you choose another one for this session or replace it in the drawing. See Missing fonts. Tick Do not show this message again to stop these messages. You can turn them on again on the Warnings page of Tools > Options > Global. Saving a drawing Choose File > Save (Ctrl+S) to write the drawing back to its file. A new drawing, or one opened from a format TraceDraw only reads, has no file yet, so Save opens the Save Drawing dialog box. Save As File > Save As (Ctrl+Shift+S) saves the drawing under another name, in another folder or in another format.  To save a drawing under a new name: Choose the folder. The list on the left has shortcuts to Home, Desktop, Documents, Downloads and Pictures, and to the drives. Up one level goes to the folder above; you can also type a folder in the path bar. Double-click a folder of the list to open it; click a file to take its name. Type the File name. The extension of the chosen type is added. Choose Save as type: TraceDraw (*.tdraw) or CDR files (*.cdr). Choose the Version. For TraceDraw files it is the version of the format, newest first. For .cdr files it is the version of the file, from 27 down to 7; an older program can only open a version as old as itself or older. The version you choose stays with the drawing, so Save writes it again without asking. Choose what goes into the file with the drawing: For .cdr files from version 16, Embed colour profile stores the drawing's CMYK profile in the file. Embed fonts (off at first) stores the fonts the text uses, when their licence allows it, in TraceDraw files and in .cdr files from version 16. The box shows how much the fonts add to the file. Tick it for drawings that go to a computer that may not have the fonts. A note under the box names any font the file will not carry and why: its licence forbids embedding, or there is no font file to embed (the text is drawn by a stand-in font, or the font is in a collection file). For TraceDraw files on the desktop, Package saves the drawing in a folder of its name with the pictures it links to, the font files and a report, and Include a PDF adds a PDF. See Packaging a drawing. These choices are kept for the next time. Optionally fill in Title, Subject and a Rating (click the lit last star again to take it off). They are the drawing's properties, also shown in Document properties. Click Save or press Enter. If the file exists, TraceDraw asks whether to Replace it. The dialog box starts in the drawing's folder, else in the folder you saved to last, else in your documents folder. A drawing opened from a .cdr file or another format starts in that file's folder with its name, so saving in the same format replaces it. In the file list, New folder makes a folder and lets you type its name at once; F2 or a right-click renames a folder or file; typing letters jumps to the entries that start with them, and Enter opens the folder picked. A folder typed in the path bar is taken without pressing Enter first. Note: In the browser version every save is a download: the dialog box keeps the name, type, version and properties, and the browser puts the file in its downloads folder. Other ways to save: File > Save as Template saves a template (see Templates), Export writes other formats (see Exporting), Publish to PDF writes a PDF (see Publishing to PDF), Send To saves a PDF to your desktop or documents folder or attaches it to an email, Package puts the drawing, its pictures and its fonts into one folder (see Packaging a drawing), and GitHub keeps drawings in a GitHub repository (see GitHub). Revert goes back to the version last saved. Closing drawings Choose File > Close (Ctrl+F4), click the close button on the drawing's tab, or middle-click the tab. Close All closes every drawing, and Exit (Alt+F4) closes TraceDraw. When a drawing has unsaved changes, TraceDraw asks whether to save them first: Yes saves (asking for a name if the drawing has no file yet), No closes without saving, and Cancel keeps the drawing open. When several drawings have changes, it asks about each one; Cancel stops.  Auto-backu

h: Undoing and redoing The Undo panel Zooming The Zoom tool Panning Views
x: Undoing, zooming and panning You can undo any change, and look at your drawing at any zoom level and from any position. Zooming and panning never change the drawing. Undoing and redoing Edit > Undo (Ctrl+Z) takes back the last change; Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z) does it again. The arrows beside Undo and Redo on the standard toolbar list the steps. Choose a step to undo or redo every change up to it. Repeat applies the last command again, for example to the next object you select. A move, resize or rotation is repeated about the selected object's own centre, side or corner, so the object turns or grows where it is instead of moving away. The Undo panel The Undo panel lists every change of the drawing, oldest first. Click a step to take the drawing back to how it was after that step; click a later step to go forward again. Open it from Window > Panels.  Zooming Turn the mouse wheel to zoom in or out about the pointer. Use the zoom box on the standard toolbar: type a level, or choose one from its list (10% to 1600%), or zoom to the selection, all objects, the page, the page width or the page height. View > Zoom In and Zoom Out zoom one step; Zoom To Fit (F4) shows all objects, Zoom To Page (Shift+F4) the page and Zoom To Selected (Shift+F2) the selection. A trackpad pinch zooms, and on a touch screen two fingers pan and pinch with any tool. The Zoom tool Choose the Zoom tool (Z or F2), then: click to zoom in by two at that point; Shift+click or right-click to zoom out by two; drag a rectangle to zoom so the rectangle fills the window. With F2 the tool zooms once: after the click or the rectangle, the tool you had before comes back. With Z it stays until you choose another tool. Double-click the tool's button to zoom to fit all objects. Panning Hold the middle mouse button and drag, with any tool. Choose the Pan tool (H) and drag. Ctrl+wheel scrolls up and down, Alt+wheel sideways. Use the scroll bars, which cover the page and one page size around it. Hold the Navigator button in the corner between the scroll bars and move the pointer over the thumbnail of the page. PgUp and PgDn go to the previous and next page. To make the wheel scroll instead of zoom, change the mouse wheel action on the Zoom/Pan page of Tools > Options > Tools. Then the wheel scrolls, Shift+wheel scrolls sideways and Ctrl+wheel zooms. See Tool options. Views The View menu chooses how objects are drawn: Wireframe shows outlines only, Normal and Enhanced draw fills and effects, and Pixels shows the drawing as the pixels of an export. Full-screen Preview shows the page alone on the screen; press any key to come back. Preview Selected Only limits that preview to the selection. The View menu also shows or hides the rulers, grids, guidelines, bleed and printable area; see Rulers, grids and guidelines.

h: Was das Andockfenster zeigt Zwischen Seiten wechseln
x: Das Andockfenster Hinweise Das Andockfenster Hinweise erklärt das Werkzeug, das Sie gerade verwenden, während Sie es verwenden. Es ist anfangs geöffnet, neben Eigenschaften und Objekte; öffnen Sie es erneut mit Hilfe > Hinweise oder über Fenster > Bereiche.  Was das Andockfenster zeigt Die Startseite stellt das Andockfenster vor und listet Themen auf, etwa Linien zeichnen, Formen, Objekte auswählen, verschieben und drehen, Effekte, Umrisse, Füllungen, Text, KI und Hilfe erhalten. Jedes Thema ist ein Link. Eine Themenseite erklärt das Thema und listet die passenden Werkzeuge auf, jedes mit Symbol, Namen und Funktion. Klicken Sie auf ein Werkzeug, um seine Seite zu sehen. Eine Werkzeugseite erklärt die Verwendung des Werkzeugs, eine Anweisung pro Zeile mit den Tasten in Fettschrift, und verweist auf das Thema, das das Werkzeug auflistet. Eine Objektseite erscheint, wenn Sie etwas auswählen: Sie nennt, was Sie ausgewählt haben (eine Kurve, ein Rechteck, Text, eine Bitmap, eine Gruppe, einen Beschneidungsrahmen, eine Überblendung, eine Maßlinie usw. oder mehrere Objekte), sagt, was Sie damit tun können, listet die passenden Werkzeuge auf und zeigt, was die Eigenschaftsleiste dafür bietet. Jede Seite endet mit Mehr erfahren, einem Link zu der Seite dieser Hilfe, die das Werkzeug oder Thema ausführlich erklärt. Zwischen Seiten wechseln Wenn Sie ein anderes Werkzeug wählen, zeigt das Andockfenster die Seite dieses Werkzeugs. Die Leiste unten im Andockfenster hat links Start und rechts Zurück und Vorwärts, wie ein Webbrowser. Wenn Sie ein Objekt auswählen, zeigt das Andockfenster dessen Seite; ein Klick auf eine leere Stelle, sodass nichts mehr ausgewählt ist, bringt die Seite des aktiven Werkzeugs zurück. Beim Zeichnen mit einem Zeichenwerkzeug bleibt die Werkzeugseite sichtbar; klicken Sie auf das Objekt, um seine Seite zu sehen.

h: Die Meldung beim Start Unterschiede zur Desktopversion
x: Die Browserversion Maschinelle Übersetzung: Diese Seite kann hinter der englischen Fassung zurückliegen. Sie können TraceDraw in einem Webbrowser verwenden, ohne etwas zu installieren. Es ist dasselbe Programm wie die Desktopversion, für den Browser erstellt, sodass Menüs, Werkzeuge und Dateien dieselben sind.  Die Meldung beim Start Bei jedem Öffnen der Seite erklärt eine Meldung, dass die Browserversion dasselbe Programm wie die Desktopversion ist und was sich unterscheidet. OK (oder Enter) schließt sie; eine zweite Schaltfläche öffnet die Downloads der Desktopversion. Unterschiede zur Desktopversion Geschwindigkeit. Große Zeichnungen, aufwendige Effekte, Nachzeichnen, Mosaike und große Exporte sind langsamer und halten die Seite beschäftigt, bis sie fertig sind. Die Desktopversion läuft mit voller Geschwindigkeit. Dateien. Öffnen und Importieren verwenden die Dateiauswahl des Browsers; Speichern, Exportieren und Drucken laden eine Datei herunter. Zuletzt verwendete Zeichnungen werden nicht aufgelistet, weil ein Browser eine hochgeladene Datei nicht erneut öffnen kann. Schriften. Die Seite bringt eigene Schriften mit und lädt weitere, wenn Ihr Text sie zum ersten Mal benötigt. Einstellungen werden in diesem Browser auf diesem Computer gespeichert. Tasten. Solange die Zeichnung den Fokus hat, gehen die Tastenkürzel des Programms an TraceDraw statt an den Browser, außer den Tasten für die Zwischenablage, Neu laden und den Entwicklertools des Browsers. Ctrl+N, Ctrl+T und Ctrl+W bleiben immer beim Browser; verwenden Sie daher das Menü Datei, um Zeichnungen zu erstellen und zu schließen. Bildschirme. Sie eignet sich für einen Desktopbrowser mit Maus und Tastatur. Verwenden Sie auf einem Tablet den Touch-Arbeitsbereich (siehe Arbeitsbereiche); ein Telefonbildschirm ist zum Bearbeiten zu klein. Makros. Makroprojekte werden nur in der Desktop-Version geladen und ausgeführt. Im Browser zeigt jeder Makrobefehl einen Hinweis darauf, mit einer Schaltfläche zu den Desktop-Downloads. Aktualisierungen. Die Browserversion ist immer die neueste; es gibt nichts zu installieren. Automatische Sicherung und Sitzungswiederherstellung sind Funktionen der Desktopversion. Als App installiert, behält sie die zuletzt verwendete Version und übernimmt eine neue beim nächsten Start, nachdem alle ihre Fenster geschlossen waren; siehe Tablets und die Android-App. Stiftdruck. Ein Stift arbeitet wie eine Maus, aber der Browser gibt seinen Druck nicht weiter, daher haben Striche eine gleichmäßige Breite.

h: Installing the browser version as an app The Android app Touch and pen
x: Tablets and the Android app TraceDraw runs on tablets in two ways: the browser version installed as an app (on an Android tablet, an iPad or a desktop computer), and a native app for Android tablets, phones and Chromebooks. Both are the same editor as the desktop version, with the same menus, tools and files. Installing the browser version as an app The browser version can be installed from the browser. It then opens full screen with the TraceDraw icon, without the browser's address bar and tabs, in any orientation, and keeps clear of a notch or rounded screen corners. Android tablet (Chrome, Edge, Samsung Internet): open the page, then the browser's menu and Install app or Add to Home screen. Chrome may also offer it in a bar under the address bar. iPad (Safari): open the page, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. Desktop (Chrome, Edge): click the install icon at the right end of the address bar, or choose Install TraceDraw in the browser's menu. Once it has been opened, the installed app starts without a network connection, at the version you last used (fonts fetched from the web still need a connection the first time your text uses them). A new version is taken the next time the app starts after all its pages and windows were closed. It is the same program as the browser version, so the differences listed in The browser version apply. The Android app The Android app is TraceDraw built for 64-bit ARM tablets and phones and for Chromebooks with Intel or AMD processors. Its installation files (APK) are attached to the releases and to the nightly builds of the project on GitHub. The app does not check for updates itself; Help > Updates opens its store page. A new installation starts in the Touch workspace: larger bars and buttons, no rulers, panels or status bar; two fingers pan and a pinch zooms. Window > Workspace picks another one, and the choice is kept. See Workspaces. What works differently: Files. Open, Import, Save, Save As, Export and Publish to PDF go through the system's document picker. Save writes an opened document back in place. The Save Drawing dialog box asks only for the name, type and version; the system then asks where to save. Recent drawings reopen from the list and the Welcome Screen, as on the desktop. Clipboard. Text goes through the system clipboard: objects copied in TraceDraw paste in other apps as text, and text copied elsewhere pastes as text. Pictures copied in other apps are not read yet. Fonts. The system's fonts are used. Keyboard. A physical or Bluetooth keyboard works with the shortcuts. Help pages open in the browser. Not available on Android: printing, Send To, editing a bitmap in another program, and choosing a folder (such as an export folder or a font folder). Touch and pen On a touch screen, a finger or a pen works the canvas, the toolbox, the bars and the menus. Tap to click, drag to draw or move. In the Touch workspace two fingers pan and a pinch zooms. For pen pressure on desktop systems, see Drawing with a graphics tablet.

h: Before you start: the token Opening a drawing from GitHub Saving a drawing to GitHub When GitHub refuses a save Opening an earlier version
x: Keeping drawings on GitHub TraceDraw can open drawings from a GitHub repository and save them back as commits, on the desktop and in the browser. Each save becomes a version in the repository's history, which you can open again later. The commands are in File > GitHub. Before you start: the token Public repositories open without a token. To open private ones and to save, create a fine-grained personal access token on GitHub with read and write access to the contents of the repository, and paste it in the Token field. The token is kept while TraceDraw runs. Tick Remember the token on this computer to keep it for the next time; it is then stored in plain text in your preferences (in the browser, in that browser's storage). The dialog boxes also remember the last repository, branch and path. Opening a drawing from GitHub Choose File > GitHub > Open from GitHub. Type the Repository as owner/name or its github.com address. Type the Branch, or leave it empty for main. Type the path of the File in the repository, for example art/logo.tdraw. Click OK. The drawing opens in a new tab, named after the file. It remembers where it came from and which version it was.  Saving a drawing to GitHub For a drawing opened from GitHub, Save (Ctrl+S) saves it back. For any drawing, choose File > GitHub > Save to GitHub. Check the repository, branch and path. Write a Commit message that says what changed (it starts as "Update" and the file name). Click OK. The drawing is saved as a .tdraw file, with its fonts, as a new commit on that branch. Save As still saves a file on your computer.  When GitHub refuses a save If the file changed on GitHub since you opened it, or a file already exists at that path and your drawing did not come from it, GitHub refuses the save and the dialog box says so. Save under another path or branch, or open the newer version first. The dialog box also explains other problems: a token that is refused or has no access, too many requests, a repository, branch or file that does not exist, a path that is a folder, a file that is not a drawing, or a drawing larger than 100 MB. Opening an earlier version For a drawing opened from GitHub, choose File > GitHub > History. The box lists the commits that changed the file, newest first, with their short id, date, author and message. Select one and click Open: that version opens as a new drawing, named after the file and the commit, which is not tied to GitHub.

Linien, Formen und Umrisse Alles, was Sie in TraceDraw zeichnen, besteht aus Linien und Formen. Diese Seiten erklären die Werkzeuge, die sie zeichnen, wie Sie sie Knoten für Knoten umformen, wie Sie sie kombinieren und zerschneiden, und wie Sie den Umriss einstellen, der ihre Kanten zeichnet. h: Freehand 2-Point Line Bezier Pen B-Spline Polyline 3-Point Curve Continuing a curve The property bar Editing curves afterwards
x: Drawing lines and curves A line in TraceDraw is a curve: a path made of segments that join at nodes. Segments can be straight or curved. A curve can be open, with two ends, or closed, when its end meets its start, and then it can be filled. The curve tools are in the Curve flyout of the toolbox. Every one of them draws a curve with the default fill and outline of new objects; change them afterwards in the Properties panel or with the color palette. Freehand The Freehand tool (F5) draws a line where you drag, like a pencil. Choose the Freehand tool. Drag on the page. Release the button to finish. TraceDraw follows the pointer and smooths the line when you release it. The smoothing (0 to 100, 50 at first) on the property bar sets how much: a higher value gives fewer nodes and a softer line. When you are zoomed in, the line keeps more detail. To draw a straight line with this tool, click where the line starts and click again where it ends. Hold Ctrl to keep the line to steps of 15 degrees. Esc drops the first click. With a graphics tablet, the pen's pressure sets the width of the line along it; see Drawing with a graphics tablet. 2-Point Line The 2-Point Line tool draws one straight segment: press where it starts and release where it ends, or click twice. Hold Ctrl to keep it to steps of 15 degrees. Bezier The Bezier tool draws precise curves node by node. Choose the Bezier tool. Click to place a corner node (a cusp), or drag to place a smooth node and pull out its handles, which set the direction and the bend of the curve. Go on placing nodes. Double-click or press Enter to finish. To close the curve, click its first node. Esc throws away the curve you are drawing. Hold Ctrl to place the next node in steps of 15 degrees from the last one, or to turn a handle in such steps. Every node snaps to what snapping is set to; see Snapping. While you drag a handle, hold C to make the node a cusp (only the outgoing handle follows), or Alt to move the node itself. Click the last node again to make it a cusp. A handle pulled out of the drawing window (over a panel or a toolbar) ends where you let go. While you draw, Ctrl+Z takes back the last node or handle, one at a time, and Ctrl+Shift+Z puts them back. A finished curve keeps these steps: undoing goes back to drawing it, with the tool chosen again and a line going on from the last node left, so you can undo node by node and draw on at once. What you are drawing shows over any color: the segments placed so far lie on a white line, and the handles are dashed in blue and white. Pen The Pen tool places nodes the same way as the Bezier tool: click for a corner node, drag for a smooth node, double-click or Enter to finish, click the first node to close. While the button is down, the handle follows the pointer, so you see the curve take shape. Its pointer is a pen nib whose tip is where the node goes. Two options sit on its property bar (and on the Curve tools page of the tool options): Preview mode (on at first): a solid blue line on a white one runs from the last node to the pointer, so you see the next segment before you click. Add and delete nodes automatically (on at first): with a curve selected and no curve being drawn, a click on a segment adds a node and a click on a node deletes it. While you draw a curve, every click places the next node, also on a segment or a node of a curve, so drawing never changes other curves by accident. With no curve being drawn, the Pen and Bezier tools also edit the selected curve: drag a node that is not an end node to move it, as with the Shape tool. B-Spline The B-Spline tool draws smooth curves from control points, without handles. Click to place each control point. The curve follows the points, starting at the first and ending at the last, and always stays inside them. While you draw, the control points show as a dashed line. Double-click or press Enter to finish. Click the first point (once there are three) to close the curve into a smooth loop. The result is an ordinary curve; the control points are not kept. Polyline The Polyline tool draws straight segments one after the other: click to add each corner, and double-click or press Enter to finish. Hold Ctrl to keep each segment to steps of 15 degrees. 3-Point Curve The 3-Point Curve tool draws an arc through three points: Drag from where the curve starts to where it ends. Hold Ctrl to keep this line to steps of 15 degrees, for a level arc. Move the pointer to bend the curve, and click the point it passes through. Hold Ctrl for a bow, a part of a circle that stands evenly on the line. Continuing a curve To add to an open curve, select it, then draw with the Freehand, 2-Point Line, Bezier, Pen, B-Spline or Polyline tool starting (or ending) on one of its end nodes. The new line becomes part of the curve: it runs on from that end; when it ends on the curve's other end, the curve closes; when it ends on an end of another part of the same curve, the two parts join. The Bezier and Pen tools also go on from an open curve that is not selected: press on one of its end nodes to select it and draw on. The next segment leaves smoothly, along the mirror of the curve's last handle; drag from the end node to pull a new handle instead, or click the end node a second time to make it a cusp, so the next segment leaves it straight. The pointer shows a node with a line going on from it when you are over an end node, and a ring when a click would close the curve. The curve keeps its look and stays selected, and the change is one undo step. Closed curves, several selected objects and objects inside groups are never continued. The distance that counts as "on the node" is set on the Curve tools page of the tool options; see Tool options. The property bar While a curve tool is active, the property bar shows the position, size, scale, angle and mirror buttons of the selection, its outline width, line style and start and end arrowheads, and a button that closes an open curve. h: Brush Strokes Modes Settings Painterly Brush Brushes and settings
x: Brush strokes and painterly brushes Brush strokes turn a line you draw into a filled shape with a varying width, like ink from a pen or a brush. Painterly brushes paint the outline of an object with marks of chalk, ink, watercolor and other media. Brush Strokes The Brush Strokes tool (I) draws strokes in one of five modes. A Preset, Brush, Calligraphic or Expression stroke stays the path you drew, an open curve of a few nodes, with the brush as its live outline: edit its nodes with the Shape tool afterwards and the brush follows. The Sprayer makes objects instead. To draw a brush stroke: Choose the Brush Strokes tool. Choose a mode and its settings on the property bar or in the Brush Strokes panel. Drag on the page. To turn existing curves into strokes, select them and click Apply to curve in the Brush Strokes panel; the curve stays a curve with the brush as its outline. With a graphics tablet, the pen's pressure sets the width of Preset, Brush and Expression strokes; see Drawing with a graphics tablet.  Modes Calligraphic: a flat nib of the given width, held at the given angle (45 degrees at first). The stroke is thinnest where you move along the nib and widest across it. Preset: a stroke whose width follows a profile: taper both ends (at first), taper start, taper end, bulge, wave or flat. The width is the widest point. Brush: a preset profile with a rough, dry-brush edge. Expression: the width follows the pen's pressure, or with a mouse your speed: slow strokes are wide. The pressure setting scales the effect. Sprayer: shapes (circles, squares, stars, hearts or leaves) placed along the line every spacing (8 mm at first), each between 70% and 100% of the width. Settings Width: 3 mm at first. Angle: the nib's angle, for Calligraphic. Smoothing: 0 to 100 (25 at first). Higher values smooth out wobbles. Pressure: how much the width follows the pen pressure (0.5 at first), for Preset, Brush and Expression. Spacing: for Sprayer. Painterly Brush The Painterly Brush tool, in the same flyout, paints a line made of brush marks. The brushstroke is an ordinary curve with no fill: the Shape tool reshapes it, the outline color colors it, and the marks follow. To paint a stroke: Choose the Painterly Brush tool. Choose a brush, a size and a transparency on the property bar. Drag on the page. To paint the outline of existing objects, click them to select them, then pick a brush: their outlines are painted with it. Changing the size or the transparency changes their brushstrokes. Clear Brushstroke gives the selected objects their plain outline back. Brushes and settings Brush: dry media (Chalk, which is the first, Charcoal, Soft Pastel), wet media (Ink Wash, Watercolour, Dry Brush) and textures (Bristle, Fur, Spray, Speckle, Cloud, Silk Ribbon). Brush size: 0.1 to 200 mm, 5 mm at first. Transparency: 0 to 100%, 20% at first. Most brushes thin out towards both ends. The marks are laid the same way each time the stroke is drawn, exported or printed. With "Scale with object" on, the marks grow and shrink with the object. In SVG and PDF exports the marks become filled shapes with their transparency.

h: Drawing with pressure Turning pressure off Which systems give the pressure
x: Drawing with a graphics tablet A graphics tablet's pen moves the pointer and clicks like a mouse, so every tool works with it. Where the system also tells TraceDraw how hard the pen presses, the Freehand and Brush Strokes tools let that pressure set the width of the stroke: press lightly for a thin line, harder for a wide one. The mouse draws an even width, as before. Drawing with pressure Choose the Freehand tool, or the Brush Strokes tool in the Preset, Brush or Expression mode. Draw with the pen, pressing harder where the stroke should be wider. Freehand: the new line gets a variable-width outline that follows the pressure along it. A feather-light touch gives a hairline, full pressure the full outline width of new lines. You can edit the line with the Shape tool and its outline in the Properties panel, as any line with a variable width (see Outlines). Brush Strokes: the pen scales the width of Preset, Brush and Expression strokes. The Pressure setting of the Brush Strokes panel (0.5 at first) says how much the width follows the pen: at 0.5 a stroke with no pressure is half as wide as at full pressure; at 1 it goes from nothing to the full width. Preset and Brush keep their shape along the stroke (a taper, a wave) and scale it by the pen; Expression takes the pen's pressure in place of the drawing speed. Calligraphic strokes and the sprayer's objects keep their size. The stroke shows as a thin line while you draw and takes its widths when you lift the pen. Apply to a curve in the Brush Strokes panel has no pen, so it builds the stroke without pressure. Turning pressure off The pressure is on at first. To draw with the pen at an even width, turn off Pen pressure sets the width of Freehand and Brush Strokes drags under Graphics tablet on the Curve tools page of Tools > Options > Tools. Which systems give the pressure Windows 8 and later yes yes Linux with X11 yes yes Linux with Wayland no (see below) no macOS yes yes Browser version yes no On a Wayland desktop (the default of several Linux systems) the pen does not reach TraceDraw yet. Start TraceDraw with tracedraw --x11 from a terminal: the window then opens through XWayland, where the pen moves the pointer, clicks and reports its pressure. Tip: For more control over the stroke afterwards, draw with pressure, then adjust the width nodes with the Variable Outline tool.

h: Shape Recognition Sketch
x: Sketching and shape recognition Two tools turn quick hand-drawn strokes into clean objects: the Shape Recognition tool recognizes the shape you meant, and the Sketch tool builds a smooth line from several strokes. Shape Recognition The Shape Recognition tool (Shift+S) turns a freehand stroke into the shape it looks like, as you drew it: a tilted rectangle stays tilted. Choose the Shape Recognition tool. Draw the shape in one stroke. A stroke whose ends come close together is taken as closed. Release the button. What you get: An open stroke that is nearly straight becomes a straight line; otherwise a smooth curve. A closed stroke with four corners near right angles becomes a rectangle. When it is nearly level, it comes out level. A closed, rounded stroke becomes an ellipse, level when nearly level and never tilted when nearly round. A closed stroke with three corners becomes a triangle, and one with four other corners a four-sided shape. Anything else becomes a smooth closed curve. The new object takes the default fill and outline and is selected. On the property bar, Shape recognition sets how readily strokes become shapes, and Smoothing how much the leftover curves are smoothed. Each is None, Lowest, Low, Medium (at first), High or Highest. With recognition at None, every stroke stays a curve. Sketch The Sketch tool (S) lets you build a line from several short strokes, as you would with a pencil. Choose the Sketch tool. Draw a stroke. It is smoothed and selected. Draw the next stroke starting near the end of the first. With Join on, it is added to the same curve. On the property bar, Join adds a stroke to the selected open curve when it starts close enough to its end; the distance beside it sets how close (5 mm at first). Smoothing sets how much each stroke is smoothed, from None to Highest.

h: Drawing with a box Rectangle Corners 3-Point Rectangle Ellipse 3-Point Ellipse The Corners panel
x: Drawing rectangles and ellipses Rectangles and ellipses stay rectangles and ellipses after you draw them: you can change their corners, turn an ellipse into a pie or an arc, and still resize them freely. To edit them node by node, convert them to curves with Object > Convert to Curves. Drawing with a box The Rectangle, Ellipse, polygon, star, spiral, graph paper, common shapes and action lines tools all draw by dragging a box. While you drag, the object itself follows the pointer, with the settings of the property bar. Hold Ctrl to draw a square, a circle or a regular shape. Hold Shift to draw from the center out. You can press or release it while dragging. The start and end points snap to what snapping is set to. The new object takes the default fill and outline (no fill and a thin black outline at first) and is selected. To change those defaults, see Object styles and defaults. Rectangle Choose the Rectangle tool (F6) and drag from one corner to the opposite one. Double-click the tool's button to draw a rectangle the size of the page; hold Shift while you double-click to frame the selection instead. Corners The property bar sets the corners of the selected rectangles, or of new ones when nothing is selected: The corner style: Round (a quarter circle), Scalloped (a quarter circle cut inwards) or Chamfered (a straight cut). The four sizes: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right. The size is the radius, or for a chamfer how far from the corner the cut starts. A corner is at most half the shorter side. Edit corners together (the lock, on at first) gives all four the size you type in one. Relative corner scaling (on at first): the corners grow and shrink with the rectangle. Turned off, they keep their size when you resize the rectangle and stay round when you stretch it. You can also drag a corner node with the Shape tool to round all corners at once. 3-Point Rectangle The 3-Point Rectangle tool draws a rectangle at an angle: Drag to draw the base line, at any angle (hold Ctrl for steps of 15 degrees). Move the pointer to set the height and click. Ellipse Choose the Ellipse tool (F7) and drag a box. Hold Ctrl for a circle. On the property bar, choose Ellipse, Pie or Arc. For a pie or an arc, set the start and end angles (in degrees, counterclockwise from the right) and the direction. You can also drag the node of an ellipse with the Shape tool to make a pie (drag inside) or an arc (drag outside). 3-Point Ellipse The 3-Point Ellipse tool draws an ellipse at an angle: Drag to draw the center line of the ellipse, at any angle (hold Ctrl for steps of 15 degrees). Move the pointer to set the height and click. The Corners panel The Corners panel rounds, scallops or chamfers the corners of curves, which the rectangle settings cannot do. Open it from Window > Panels.  Select one or more objects. Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and text become curves when the corners are cut. Choose the Operation: Fillet (a round arc that touches both sides), Scallop (a notch, a quarter of a circle around the corner) or Chamfer (a straight cut). Set the Radius for a fillet or scallop (2 mm at first), or the Chamfer distance for a chamfer: the first distance along the side the path comes in on and the second along the side it leaves on. Equal distances keeps them the same. The result shows as a dashed outline on the drawing. Click Apply. A corner is a node where two segments meet at an angle; smooth nodes are not corners. With the Shape tool and some nodes selected, only those corners are cut. A corner whose sides are too short for the cut is skipped. On a stretched object a fillet or scallop still comes out round, with the radius measured on the page.

t: Drawing polygons, stars, spirals and other shapes
h: Polygon Star Spiral Common Shapes Action Lines Graph Paper
x: Drawing polygons, stars, spirals and other shapes These tools draw ready-made shapes by dragging a box. As with rectangles, hold Ctrl to keep the shape regular and Shift to draw from the center; see Drawing with a box. Polygon The Polygon tool (Y) draws a regular polygon. Set the number of points (3 to 500, 5 at first) on the property bar before or after drawing. The first corner is at the top center. Polygons are symmetric: when you move one node with the Shape tool, the matching nodes of every side move with it, so you can turn a pentagon into a flower in one drag. Star The Star tool draws a star. Its property bar starts with two buttons that choose what it draws: Star: a star with the given number of points (5 at first) and sharpness (0.5 at first; 0 makes a polygon, 1 the thinnest spikes). Complex star: a star whose sides cross, made by joining each point to one further on (9 points and sharpness 2 at first). Its middle stays empty. With some numbers of points it is made of several closed shapes, as six points give two triangles. Spiral The Spiral tool (A) draws a spiral, an open curve. On the property bar set the revolutions (1 to 100, 4 at first) and choose a symmetrical spiral, whose turns are evenly spaced, or a logarithmic one, whose turns grow further apart. Hold Ctrl to draw a round spiral. Common Shapes The Common Shapes tool draws ready-made shapes. Click the shape button on the property bar to choose one from five sets: Basic shapes: parallelogram, trapezoid, diamond, triangles, hexagon, octagon, plus, heart, lightning, crescent, ring, cylinder, cube, frame, teardrop, smiley face and no symbol. Arrows: in every direction, chevron, pentagon, notched, striped and bent arrows. Flowchart: process, decision, data, document, terminator, connector, storage and the other usual symbols. Banners: ribbons, waves, scroll, explosion, burst and pennant. Callouts: rectangle, rounded, oval, cloud and line callouts. Then drag a box. The shape becomes one curve with the default fill and outline. Parts that should look separate, such as the faces of a cube, are separate parts of the curve, and holes such as the middle of a ring stay holes whatever the fill. Action Lines The Action Lines tool draws speed lines in a comic-book style: a group of lines (2 to 500, 12 at first) that are parallel (at first) or radial. Their lengths vary, but the same box always gives the same lines. Graph Paper The Graph Paper tool (D) draws a grid of cells: a group of rectangles that fill the box exactly. Set the rows and columns (4 by 3 at first) on the property bar. Hold Ctrl for square cells. The default points, revolutions, rows and columns are also on the tool pages of the options; see Tool options.

t: Shaping curves with the Shape tool
h: Nodes and segments Selecting nodes Moving nodes and bending segments Rounding corners of curves The property bar Aligning nodes Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and other objects
x: Shaping curves with the Shape tool The Shape tool (F10) edits the nodes and segments of a curve: you move nodes, bend segments, add and delete nodes and change how each node joins its segments. Nodes and segments Select a curve with the Shape tool. Its outline shows in the node color, its nodes as small markers, and the first node of each part of the curve as a slightly larger triangle. A selected node shows its control handles: dashed lines that end in an arrow at the control point. A node is one of three types: Cusp: the segments meet at an angle; each handle moves on its own. Smooth: the curve passes through without a corner; the two handles stay in line. Symmetrical: smooth, with both handles the same length. The pointer shows what a press would take: a small square over a node, a dot over a control handle, a wave over a segment. Selecting nodes Click a node to select it alone; Ctrl+click adds it or takes it out of the selection. Shift+click selects every node from the last selected one to the one you click. Drag a marquee around nodes. The property bar's selection mode chooses a rectangular or a freehand marquee. Tab and Shift+Tab select the next or previous node; Home and End the first or last. Ctrl+A, the select all nodes button, or a double-click on the tool's button selects every node. Moving nodes and bending segments Drag a node to move the selected nodes. Hold Ctrl to move only horizontally or vertically. Nodes snap like drawing points, also to the other nodes and segments of their own curve. Drag a segment to bend it: the point you grab follows the pointer while the nodes at its ends stay. A straight segment becomes curved. Cusp nodes at its ends stay cusp, and their other handles stay where they are. Drag a control handle to change the bend. While you drag a node, a segment or a handle, the page keeps the picture it had before the drag and the curve follows the pointer as the thin line the tool draws over it. The outline, with its width nodes, brush, arrowheads and effects, is drawn again once, when you release the button. The arrow keys nudge the selected nodes (Shift for a larger step, Ctrl for a smaller one). Double-click a segment to add a node there, a node to delete it. Click a segment to mark a spot, then press + to add a node there. Delete or - deletes the selected nodes; + adds a node in the middle of each segment that ends at them. Neighbouring nodes deleted together leave one curve fitted to the old outline, so the shape keeps its general form. With nodes selected, C switches them between cusp and smooth, S between smooth and symmetrical, and Y makes them symmetrical. With nodes selected, Ctrl+C copies the segments between them as new curves, Ctrl+X cuts them out, and Ctrl+D duplicates them. Right-click a node or segment for a menu of the commands below. With several objects selected, the object picked last shows its outline in the node color (blue) and the others in the secondary node color (red), also while a node is dragged, so you can tell them apart. End nodes of two different objects are not joined, by Join nodes or by dropping one on the other: combine the objects first (Object > Combine, Ctrl+L), then join their ends. Rounding corners of curves Rings inside the corners of a curve let you round a corner by dragging. They are off at first, so they do not get in the way of editing nodes; turn on Show corner rounding rings on curve nodes (Shape tool) on the Nodes and Handles page of Tools > Options > TraceDraw to use them. Drag the ring of a corner between two straight sides to round it. A rounded corner keeps its ring: drag it again to change the radius, further in or back to a sharp corner. This also works on corners rounded in saved drawings and with the Corners panel. On a stretched curve the corners come out round on the page, not oval. Rectangles round their corners by their own nodes, whatever this option says. The property bar Selection mode: rectangular or freehand marquee. Add node and Delete node. Join nodes joins two end nodes into one; Break curve splits the curve at the selected node. Convert to line and Convert to curve make the segment ending at the node straight or curved. Cusp, Smooth and Symmetrical set the node type. Reverse direction turns the curve round; Extend curve to close joins two selected end nodes with a straight segment; Extract subpath makes the part of the selected node a curve of its own; Close curve closes an open curve. Stretch and scale nodes and Rotate and skew nodes frame two or more selected nodes with handles: the corner handles scale (or rotate), the side handles stretch (or skew) only those nodes. Align nodes opens the Node Align dialog box (see below). Reflect horizontally and Reflect vertically: moving a node moves the selected nodes on the other side the mirrored way, so both sides of a shape change together. Elastic mode: the selected nodes move less the further they are from the one you drag, down to half as much for the furthest. Select all nodes. Reduce nodes removes nodes that are not needed, from the selected nodes or from the whole curve. Drag the curve smoothness slider to remove more nodes gradually. Aligning nodes To line up nodes: Select two or more nodes with the Shape tool. Click Align nodes on the property bar. In the Node Align dialog box, tick Align horizontal, Align vertical or both, and click OK. The selected nodes move onto a common horizontal or vertical line, or onto one point when both are ticked. The align keys work on the selected nodes too, two or more: L and R line them up with the leftmost or rightmost node, T and B with the top or bottom node, and E puts them on the middle of their height. Their control handles move with them. (C keeps making a node cusp here.)  Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and other objects Drag a corner node of a rectangle to round every corner; Ctrl+drag (or click it first) to round that corner only. Drag the node of an ellipse inside it to make a pie, outside it t

h: Using a shaping brush Smooth Smear Twirl Attract and Repel Smudge Roughen
x: Smoothing, smearing and roughening outlines The shaping brushes of the Shape flyout reshape the outline of an object where you drag over it, like a sculptor's tool: Smooth, Smear, Twirl, Attract and Repel, Smudge and Roughen. Using a shaping brush Select the curves to change. Other objects are converted to curves first. The brushes change only the selected objects: with nothing selected a drag does nothing, and the status bar says to select an object first. Choose the tool and set its Nib size (the radius of the brush, 10 mm at first) and its other settings on the property bar. Drag over the outline. The effect is strongest at the center of the nib and fades to nothing at its edge. Only the parts of the outline within reach change; open curves stay open and closed ones stay closed. Each drag is one undo step. The settings are kept for the next time. Smooth The Smooth tool removes wobbles and extra nodes where you drag. Rate (1 to 100%, 20% at first) sets how strongly. Smear The Smear tool (W) pulls the outline along with the pointer, as if you smeared wet paint. Pressure (1 to 100%, 100% at first) sets how far it moves. Twirl The Twirl tool turns the outline around the pointer into a swirl. Speed (1 to 100%, 50% at first) sets how fast it turns, and the direction buttons choose counterclockwise or clockwise; hold Alt or Shift while dragging to turn the other way. Holding the pointer still keeps turning. Attract and Repel The Attract and Repel tool pulls the nodes inside the nib towards the pointer, or pushes them away. Speed (1 to 100%, 50% at first) sets how fast; choose Attract or Repel on the property bar, or hold Alt or Shift while dragging to swap them. Holding the pointer still keeps going. Smudge The Smudge tool (V) smooths the outline slightly, then smears it, so it is pulled without kinks. Pressure (1 to 100%, 100% at first) sets how far. Roughen The Roughen tool (E) adds jagged spikes along the outline. Frequency (1 to 10 spikes per 10 mm, 5 at first) sets how many, and Spike size (2 mm at first) how tall. The spikes are straight, so they stay sharp.

h: Crop Knife Segment Delete Eraser
x: Cropping, cutting and erasing Four tools of the Crop flyout take parts of objects away: Crop, Knife, Segment Delete and Eraser. Each change is one undo step. Crop The Crop tool removes everything outside a rectangle. Select the objects to crop, or select nothing to crop every unlocked object on the page. Choose the Crop tool and drag the crop area. The drawing outside it is dimmed. Adjust the area: drag inside it to move it, drag one of its eight handles to resize it, or type its position and size on the property bar. Double-click inside the area, press Enter or click Crop on the property bar. To give up, press Esc, click outside the area, click Clear crop area, or choose another tool. What happens to each object: objects wholly inside stay as they are, and objects wholly outside are deleted; closed shapes are cut to the area, and open curves are cut where they cross its edge; text becomes curves first; bitmaps, tables and symbols are placed inside a frame of the area, so their content stays whole and can be taken out again (see Clip frames); groups are cropped member by member. Knife The Knife tool splits objects along a cut. Select the objects to cut, or select nothing to cut every visible object on the page. Choose the Knife tool and the kind of cut on the property bar: Two-point line (a straight cut that runs on across the objects) or Freehand (a cut that follows your drag). Drag across the objects. On the property bar, Split separates the pieces with a hairline gap, so they still meet, and Gap removes a band of the width you type. With Keep as one object, the pieces of each object stay one object made of several parts. Open curves are split where the cut crosses them. Pieces keep the fill, outline and transparency and are selected. Bitmaps, groups and text are not cut. Segment Delete The Segment Delete tool deletes the parts of outlines between the places where they cross other outlines or themselves, for example the bits of lines that stick out past a crossing. Click a part of an outline to delete it. Drag a rectangle across outlines to delete every part it touches, on all objects at once. Each part goes whole, up to the crossings at its ends, even where it reaches past the rectangle; a closed shape that nothing crosses goes whole. Choose Freehand on the property bar and drag a stroke across outlines: every part the stroke crosses is deleted, up to the crossings with other lines, in one step. Hold Alt as a drag starts to use the other way (stroke or rectangle) for that drag only. Rectangles, ellipses and polygons become curves; a closed shape that loses a part opens, and an object with nothing left is deleted. Eraser The Eraser tool (X) rubs out parts of objects. Select the objects to erase, or select nothing to erase the object you start dragging on. Choose the Eraser tool. Set the thickness (6.35 mm at first) and the round or square nib on the property bar. Drag over the objects. A click erases one dot. Erased objects become curves; an object erased completely is deleted. Double-click an object with the tool to delete it whole. Bitmaps, groups and clip frames are not erased. The defaults of the eraser are on the Eraser page of the tool options; see Tool options.

t: Combining shapes: weld, trim and intersect
h: The target and the sources The operations Open lines and pictures The Shaping panel
x: Combining shapes: weld, trim and intersect Shaping builds new shapes from overlapping objects: join them into one, cut one with another, or keep only where they overlap. The commands are in Object > Shaping, on the property bar when two or more objects are selected, and in the Shaping panel. The target and the sources The last object you select is the target: it gives the result its fill, outline and transparency. The other selected objects are the sources. To choose the target, select the sources first, then Shift+click the target. The result goes on top of the active layer and is selected. Each operation is one undo step. When there is no result (for example two objects that do not overlap), nothing changes and the status bar says so. The operations Weld 2 objects one object covering all of them Trim 2 objects the target without what the sources cover Intersect 2 objects only the area all of them share Simplify 1 object each object without what the objects above it cover Front Minus Back 2 objects the front object without the ones behind it Back Minus Front 2 objects the back object without the ones in front of it Boundary 1 object an outline around the whole selection From the menu and the property bar, Weld removes the originals, Trim keeps the sources, Intersect keeps all of them, and Boundary keeps them all. Open lines and pictures An open line cuts a shape. Trim with an open line, polyline or curve as a source crossing a closed target cuts the target along it into separate pieces, each keeping the target's fill and outline. Several lines make more pieces; a line that ends inside the shape cuts nothing, and the status bar says so. Front Minus Back and Back Minus Front split along open lines the same way. An open line as the target of Weld, Trim or Intersect is cut by the closed objects and stays open: Trim keeps the parts outside them, Intersect the part inside, and Weld adds the parts outside to the welded shape. An open line used as a source of Weld or Intersect on a closed object takes no part; to cut a shape along a line, use Trim or the Knife tool (see Cutting and erasing). A picture as the target of Trim, Intersect or Weld is cropped to the result: its frame takes the new shape and the picture shows inside it. Areas filled side by side, and the results of Weld, Trim and Intersect, meet exactly where outlines cross, with no hairline gap between them. The Shaping panel Open the Shaping panel from Object > Shaping > Shaping.  Click one of the seven picture buttons to choose the operation. The panel shows its name, a picture and what it does. For Weld, Trim and Intersect, choose what to keep: Leave original source object and Leave original target object. Each operation remembers its own choice. Select the objects, the target last. Click the button named after the operation. It stays pale until enough objects are selected, and a line says how many are needed. Related: Combine (Ctrl+L) makes several objects one curve without changing their shapes, and Break Apart splits a curve into its parts again. See Objects and layers.

h: Kurven verbinden
x: Kurven verbinden Das Andockfenster Kurven verbinden schließt die Lücken zwischen den Enden von Kurven, zum Beispiel bei Linien, die sich in einer Ecke treffen sollten, aber kurz davor aufhören. Öffnen Sie es mit Objekt > Kurven verbinden.  Kurven verbinden Wählen Sie die Kurven aus. Offene Teile innerhalb einer Kurve werden ebenfalls verbunden. Wählen Sie, wie die Enden verbunden werden: Verlängern: Beide Enden laufen in ihrer Richtung weiter, bis sie sich als Ecke treffen. Treffen sich die Richtungen vor beiden Enden nie, verbindet sie eine gerade Linie. Fase: eine gerade Linie zwischen den Enden. Abrundung: wie Verlängern, dann wird die Ecke mit dem Radius abgerundet (anfangs 2 mm). Bézierkurve: eine glatte Kurve, die in den Richtungen der Enden abgeht und ankommt. Stellen Sie die Lückentoleranz ein (anfangs 5 mm). Weiter entfernte Enden werden nicht verbunden. Klicken Sie auf Zuweisen. Das nächstgelegene Endenpaar wird zuerst verbunden, dann das nächste, bis innerhalb der Toleranz kein Paar mehr übrig ist; die beiden Enden eines Teils schließen ihn. Die verbundene Kurve übernimmt Platz, Füllung und Umriss der zuletzt ausgewählten Kurve, und die anderen Kurven werden entfernt. Liegen keine Enden nah genug beieinander, ändert sich nichts, und die Statusleiste weist darauf hin. Sie können auch zwei Endknoten einer Kurve mit dem Werkzeug Form verbinden; siehe Kurven mit dem Formwerkzeug bearbeiten. Wenn Sie vom Ende einer ausgewählten Kurve aus zeichnen, wird sie ebenfalls fortgesetzt; siehe Eine Kurve fortsetzen.

h: Opening the outline settings Outline Pen settings Outline Color Variable Outline
x: Setting outlines The outline is the line drawn along the edge of an object. You set its color, width, style, corners, line ends and arrowheads in the Outline section of the Properties panel. Opening the outline settings The Outline Pen tool (F12) opens the Outline Pen dialog box with every outline setting: color, width and its unit, style, miter limit, dashes, corners, line caps, position, arrowheads, calligraphy, Behind fill, Scale with object, the variable outline's width nodes and Overprint outline. The selected objects show each change live while the dialog box is open. OK keeps only what you changed, on every selected object, as one undo step; Cancel or Esc puts the outlines back. With nothing selected it sets the outline of new objects. The width list offers the same round widths as the property bar, in the outline unit (0.1, 0.2, 0.25 mm and so on).  Double-click the outline part of the status bar. Right-click a color of the palette to color the outline of the selection. Outline Pen settings Width: 0.2 mm for new objects. Hairline draws a line one screen or printer dot wide at every zoom. Paint: the outline can be painted like a fill: none, uniform color, gradient, pattern, texture or mesh. See Fills. Hairlines and arrowheads keep the plain outline color. Caps, the ends of open lines: Butt (at first), Round or Square. Corners: Miter (at first), Round or Bevel. The Mitre limit (45 degrees for new outlines) bevels corners sharper than it, so a thick outline on text or narrow turns does not grow long spikes. Dash: Solid, Dashed, Dotted or Dash dot. The dashes grow with the width. Arrowheads, at the Start and the End of open lines, filled in the outline color. To make your own, draw it, select it and choose Object > Create > Arrowhead. The nib stretch (0.1 to 1) and nib angle make a calligraphic outline: thinner across the nib than along it, like a flat pen. In the Properties panel they sit with the Mitre limit under the Advanced header after the common settings, closed at first unless one of them is set. Behind fill draws the outline under the fill, so only its outer half shows. Scale with object: the width grows and shrinks when you resize the object. To turn an outline into an object you can fill, choose Object > Convert Outline to Object (Ctrl+Shift+Q). The settings of new objects are explained in Object styles and defaults. Outline Color The Outline Color tool (Shift+F12) opens the Color panel to choose the outline color of the selection. See The Color panel. Variable Outline The Variable Outline tool, in the Shape flyout, makes an outline thicker or thinner along its length with width nodes. Select an object with an outline, such as a curve, a rectangle or an ellipse. An object with no outline gets a thin one. Choose the Variable Outline tool. Drag across the outline: a width node is added where you start, and the outline reaches to the pointer on both sides. Hold Shift (or Alt) as you start dragging to change only the side the pointer is on. Shift+click picks a run of nodes and Ctrl+click adds one; a drag then changes all the picked nodes. Add more nodes the same way. Between nodes the width changes smoothly. To change a node, click it and type the Left width and Right width on the property bar (left is to the left of the path's direction). Delete node or Delete removes the selected node, and Clear variable outline gives back the plain outline.

h: Placing a dimension Parallel Horizontal or Vertical Angular Segment Dimension style Dimensions that follow objects Callout
x: Dimension lines and callouts Dimension lines show the size of things in a technical drawing: a length, a horizontal or vertical distance, an angle or the length of a segment. Callouts point at something with a leader line and a label. Both stay live: when you move, scale or turn them, they are measured and drawn again. Placing a dimension Every dimension is placed in clicks, and the property bar says what to click next. While the last point is wanted, the dimension follows the pointer. Esc starts again. Points snap as drawing does, so snapping to nodes or objects gives exact measures; see Snapping. The new dimension is selected. Parallel The Parallel Dimension tool measures the straight distance between two points, at any angle: Drag from the first point to the second, or click both. Move the pointer and click where the dimension line goes. Horizontal or Vertical The Horizontal or Vertical Dimension tool measures only the horizontal or the vertical distance between two points, whichever is larger. Place it as a parallel dimension. Angular The Angular Dimension tool measures an angle: Click the vertex of the angle. Click a point on the first side, then a point on the second side. Click where the arc goes. The angle is measured counterclockwise from the first side. Segment The Segment Dimension tool measures a segment of an object: click the segment to take its two ends, then click where the dimension line goes. Dimension style The property bar shows these settings with the dimension tools and when the selection is all dimensions. Changes apply to the selected dimensions and to the next ones you make. Precision: 0 to 6 decimals (2 at first). Units: the drawing units (at first) or any other unit. Lengths follow the drawing scale, so at 1:100 a 10 mm line reads 1000 mm; see Document options. Show units: the unit after the number (the degree sign for angles). Prefix and Suffix: text before and after the number. Text: above the line (at first), in the line, or below the line. Label size: 1 to 500 points (10 at first). Font of the label (the font of new text at first) and the label color (black). Line color (black) and line width (a hairline at first, up to 50 mm), for the lines and arrowheads. Arrowheads: arrow (at first), open arrow, dot, tick or none. Round ends: round caps and joins on the lines (off). The Options menu: the extension line gap between the measured points and the extension lines (0), how far the extension lines run past the line (2 mm), horizontal text for linear dimensions (off), join lines at corners (off), which makes the extension lines and the dimension line (or an angle's arc) one line that turns a corner instead of running past it, and a corner radius (0 to 100 mm) that rounds those corners.
